draft.title: Exponential growth and decay
card: Some quantities change at a rate proportional to their size: the bigger N is, the faster it changes. This is written dN/dt = kN, and its solution is N = N₀eᵏᵗ.
N₀ is the starting amount, when t = 0. k is the constant that sets how fast N changes, and t is time.
k > 0, so N increases, as with a population in a good environment.
k < 0, so N decreases towards 0, as with a radioactive substance. Example: N = 80e^(−0.5t) starts at 80. At t = 2, N = 80e⁻¹ ≈ 29.4.
draft.remember: N = N₀eᵏᵗ: N₀ is the start, and the sign of k decides growth or decay.

a.q: A quantity follows N = 50e^(−0.2t). Which statement is true?
opts: It starts at 50 and is decaying
It starts at 50 and is growing
It starts at 0.2 and is decaying
It starts at −0.2 and is growing
a.why: N₀ = 50 is the value at t = 0, and k = −0.2 is negative, so N decays. Growing is wrong because it ignores the negative sign of k.
a.clue: Put t = 0 in, then look at the sign of k.

b.q: A colony of bacteria in a lab follows N = 200e^(0.3t), where t is in hours. What is N after 2 hours, to the nearest whole number?
b.why: N = 200e^(0.3 × 2) = 200e^0.6 ≈ 200 × 1.822 = 364. The value 260 comes from 200 + 0.3 × 2 × 100 style adding, and it is wrong because the exponent multiplies k by t before e is raised to it.
b.clue: Work out k × t first, then use e to that power.

a.best: It starts at 50 and is decaying

problems.detail: The why's account of the 260 distractor ('200 + 0.3 × 2 × 100 style adding') is muddled. The '× 100' has no clear source, and 260 is more naturally 200 × 1.3 (one step of simple 30% growth). The reason it then gives does not clearly explain that mistake.

check.summary: The card and both questions are correct: 80e⁻¹ ≈ 29.4 and 200e^0.6 ≈ 364. The only issue is that the why for question b gives a confusing account of where the 260 distractor comes from.
